base-cluster.description: Every cluster at a glance - nodes, CPU and memory trends, running pods and firing alerts per cluster - then every server and every namespace of the selected clusters.
base-cluster.title: Base clusters

observ-viz-anomaly-process.description: Every series below is compared with its own past: the rolling mean over 1d and a band 3 standard deviations wide. It owns no metrics - point it at any service.
observ-viz-anomaly-process.title: Anomaly / Process

observ-viz-anomaly-requests.description: Every series below is compared with its own past: the rolling mean over 1d and a band 3 standard deviations wide. It owns no metrics - point it at any service.
observ-viz-anomaly-requests.title: Anomaly / Requests

observ-viz-anomaly-scores.description: The anomaly exporter itself: probes per module, success and failure rates, probe duration and version. Anomaly scores live on the Anomaly scorer board.
observ-viz-anomaly-scores.title: Anomaly / Detector scores

observ-viz-burnrate-apiserver.description: How fast the error budget is being spent, and what that means for the objective. The kube-apiserver-burnrate.rules of kubernetes.cluster (or of the kubernetes-mixin) record these seven windows for the API server's own SLO, split by read and write.
observ-viz-burnrate-apiserver.title: Burn rate / Kubernetes API server

observ-viz-burnrate-pyrra.description: How fast the error budget is being spent, and what that means for the objective. Pyrra publishes the availability and the objective per SLO; the burn and the budget left follow from the two.
observ-viz-burnrate-pyrra.title: Burn rate / Pyrra SLOs

observ-viz-capacity-certificates.description: When this runs out, at the rate of the last 6h. Seconds until each cert-manager certificate expires. This one shrinks by a second per second, so the prediction is exact rather than a trend.
observ-viz-capacity-certificates.title: Capacity / Certificates

observ-viz-capacity-cluster-cpu.description: How full this is, how full it was 7d ago, and where the trend of the last 6h puts it in 4d. Cores in use against cores available, per cluster. Under 30 percent says the cluster is paid for and idle; over 70 says the next node is already late.
observ-viz-capacity-cluster-cpu.title: Capacity / Cluster CPU

observ-viz-capacity-cluster-memory.description: How full this is, how full it was 7d ago, and where the trend of the last 6h puts it in 4d. Memory in use against memory installed, per cluster.
observ-viz-capacity-cluster-memory.title: Capacity / Cluster memory

observ-viz-capacity-filesystem.description: When this runs out, at the rate of the last 6h. Free bytes per mounted filesystem, minus the ones that live in memory and cannot fill up the way a disk does.
observ-viz-capacity-filesystem.title: Capacity / Filesystems

observ-viz-capacity-memory.description: When this runs out, at the rate of the last 6h. Memory the kernel says is available - which is not free memory, it counts what the cache would give back.
observ-viz-capacity-memory.title: Capacity / Free node memory

observ-viz-capacity-node-cpu.description: How full this is, how full it was 7d ago, and where the trend of the last 6h puts it in 4d. The same question per node, which is where the imbalance shows: a cluster at 50 percent can still have a node at 95.
observ-viz-capacity-node-cpu.title: Capacity / Node CPU

observ-viz-capacity-node-memory.description: How full this is, how full it was 7d ago, and where the trend of the last 6h puts it in 4d. Memory in use against memory installed, per node.
observ-viz-capacity-node-memory.title: Capacity / Node memory

observ-viz-capacity-workload-memory.description: How full this is, how full it was 7d ago, and where the trend of the last 6h puts it in 4d. What each namespace uses against what it is allowed. Over 100 percent means it has no limits set, not that it is overcommitted.
observ-viz-capacity-workload-memory.title: Capacity / Workload memory

observ-viz-deploy-cadvisor.description: Container resource usage from cAdvisor for Kubernetes pods: CPU with throttling, memory against limits, disk IO.
observ-viz-deploy-cadvisor.title: Container runtime

observ-viz-deploy-kube-pod.description: Runtime signals for every instance matching the selected job.
observ-viz-deploy-kube-pod.title: Kubernetes pod

observ-viz-framework-django.description: A Django application as django-prometheus reports it: requests by view and method, responses by status, latency measured inside and around the middleware stack, and exceptions by view and type.
observ-viz-framework-django.title: Django

observ-viz-framework-rails.description: A Rails application as yabeda-rails reports it: requests by controller action and status, request duration percentiles, and the split of that time between the database, view rendering and outbound service calls.
observ-viz-framework-rails.title: Rails

observ-viz-golden-apiserver.description: The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and the one RED leaves out, saturation. Saturation here is the flowcontrol queue: requests waiting for a seat, which is what the API server does instead of failing when it is full.
observ-viz-golden-apiserver.title: Golden signals / Kubernetes API server

observ-viz-golden-container.description: The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and the one RED leaves out, saturation. Saturation is memory against the limit the container was given: the number that decides whether it is about to be killed.
observ-viz-golden-container.title: Golden signals / Container

observ-viz-golden-ingress-nginx.description: The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and the one RED leaves out, saturation. Saturation is the share of configured upstream connections in use, so it rises before the latency does.
observ-viz-golden-ingress-nginx.title: Golden signals / Ingress NGINX

observ-viz-golden-node.description: The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and the one RED leaves out, saturation. Traffic and errors come from the network, saturation from load against the CPUs it has - the number that leads the rest.
observ-viz-golden-node.title: Golden signals / Linux node

observ-viz-lang-dotnet.description: The .NET runtime as exposed by prometheus-net: managed heap, thread pool, exceptions and JIT activity.
observ-viz-lang-dotnet.title: .NET

observ-viz-lang-golang.description: The Go runtime as exposed by `client_golang`: goroutines, threads, heap, stack and garbage collection, plus the shared `process_*` metrics.
observ-viz-lang-golang.title: Go

observ-viz-lang-jvm.description: JVM memory pools, threads, loaded classes and garbage collection, as exposed by Micrometer or the JMX exporter.
observ-viz-lang-jvm.title: JVM

observ-viz-lang-nodejs.description: The Node.js event loop, V8 heap and handle/request counts, as exposed by `prom-client` default metrics.
observ-viz-lang-nodejs.title: Node.js

observ-viz-lang-python.description: CPython garbage collection plus the process metrics exposed by `prometheus_client` default collectors.
observ-viz-lang-python.title: Python

observ-viz-lang-rust.description: The Tokio runtime as exposed by the `tokio-metrics` crate: the worker threads, what they are busy with, and the queues behind them. Rust has no runtime of its own to measure, so this is the async executor most services run on.
observ-viz-lang-rust.title: Rust

observ-viz-process-exporter.description: Process groups from process-exporter: CPU, memory, processes and threads, file descriptors, IO and page faults per group and host, top-N tables and scrape health.
observ-viz-process-exporter.title: Process group

observ-viz-red-apiserver.description: The RED method over kubernetes api server. Every call to the API server, by resource and verb.
observ-viz-red-apiserver.title: RED / Kubernetes API server

observ-viz-red-django.description: The RED method over django. django-prometheus: responses by status, latency by view and method.
observ-viz-red-django.title: RED / Django

observ-viz-red-grafana.description: The RED method over grafana. Grafana's own HTTP handlers.
observ-viz-red-grafana.title: RED / Grafana

observ-viz-red-ingress-nginx.description: The RED method over ingress nginx. Every request the cluster ingress terminates, as the controller counts them.
observ-viz-red-ingress-nginx.title: RED / Ingress NGINX

observ-viz-red-kong.description: The RED method over kong. Every request the Kong gateway proxied, as its Prometheus plugin counts them. Point it at http_server_request_duration_seconds_* instead for a Kong exporting OpenTelemetry.
observ-viz-red-kong.title: RED / Kong

observ-viz-red-otel-http.description: The RED method over http server (opentelemetry). OpenTelemetry HTTP server semantic conventions: one histogram per request, split by route and status code.
observ-viz-red-otel-http.title: RED / HTTP server (OpenTelemetry)

observ-viz-red-prometheus-client.description: The RED method over http server (prometheus client). The `http_requests_total` / `http_request_duration_seconds` pair the Prometheus client libraries expose.
observ-viz-red-prometheus-client.title: RED / HTTP server (Prometheus client)

observ-viz-red-service-graph.description: The RED method over service graph (from traces). Tempo's metrics-generator, counting every edge between two traced services.
observ-viz-red-service-graph.title: RED / Service graph (from traces)

observ-viz-systemd.description: systemd units from node_exporter: unit state over time, active and failed counts, failed units, restarts and the overall system state.
observ-viz-systemd.title: Systemd unit

observ-viz-use-container.description: The USE method over containers (cadvisor). The same four resources per container, read from cAdvisor; saturation is what the cgroup throttled or reclaimed.
observ-viz-use-container.title: USE / Containers (cAdvisor)

observ-viz-use-node.description: The USE method over nodes (node_exporter). Brendan Gregg's USE method over node_exporter: for every resource, how busy it is, how much work is queued, and what is failing.
observ-viz-use-node.title: USE / Nodes (node_exporter)

observ-viz-windows-service.description: Windows services from the windows_exporter service collector: what each one is doing, how many run, and the ones set to start automatically that are stopped.
observ-viz-windows-service.title: Windows service

alerts.d: Nothing here says the service is broken: the shape of cpu changed against its own recent past. Compare it with the band on the board before acting, and check whether the change has an obvious cause (a deploy, a load test, a neighbour failing).
alerts.e: abs(((sum by (instance) (rate(process_cpu_seconds_total{}[5m]))) - avg_over_time((sum by (instance) (rate(process_cpu_seconds_total{}[5m])))[1d:5m])) / clamp_min(stddev_over_time((sum by (instance) (rate(process_cpu_seconds_total{}[5m])))[1d:5m]), 1e-9)) > 3
alerts.rb:
### Meaning

CPU on service is 3 standard deviations from its own 1d baseline.

Nothing here says the service is broken: the shape of cpu changed against its own recent past. Compare it with the band on the board before acting, and check whether the change has an obvious cause (a deploy, a load test, a neighbour failing).

It fires when the expression below holds for 15m.

### Impact

Nothing is broken yet, and it will be if the trend holds. Look at it this working day.

### Diagnosis

Run the alert expression and look at which series cross the threshold:

```promql
abs(((sum by (instance) (rate(process_cpu_seconds_total{}[5m]))) - avg_over_time((sum by (instance) (rate(process_cpu_seconds_total{}[5m])))[1d:5m])) / clamp_min(stddev_over_time((sum by (instance) (rate(process_cpu_seconds_total{}[5m])))[1d:5m]), 1e-9)) > 3
```

Then open this board with the same selectors: the tab that carries those metrics shows how long the series has been where it is, and the restart and deploy annotations show whether a release or a restart lines up with the change.

### Mitigation

- Confirm the target is the one you think it is: check the labels on the firing series.
- Compare against the same series on a healthy peer; a single instance out of line is a different problem from every instance moving together.
- If a deploy or restart lines up with the change, that is the first thing to undo.
- If the threshold no longer matches how this service behaves, change the rule rather than living with a permanent alert.
alerts.s: CPU on service is 3 standard deviations from its own 1d baseline.

### Meaning

slo is burning its error budget 14.4 times faster than it can afford, over 1h.

At this rate it spends the whole budget in about two days. The short window (5m) confirms it is still happening rather than something that already stopped.

Something users depend on is already broken or about to be. Treat it as an incident.

(apiserver_request:burnrate1h{} > 14.4) and (apiserver_request:burnrate5m{} > 14.4)

signals.d: How much of the work fails. Count the failures the caller sees, including the ones that answered 200 with the wrong thing where you can.

Anything above zero means the API server is shedding concurrency: requests are waiting for a seat in their priority level. How much work arrives. It gives the other three their meaning - a perfect error ratio over no traffic says nothing.

signals.d: The join / leave lines the player panels count.

signals.d: Players online across the selected game servers (the proxy excluded: a player sits on one backend at a time).
signals.e: sum(last_over_time({cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"minecraft-java-$server", container!~"minecraft-java-.*proxy"} |~ `joined the game|left the game|\[connected player\] .* has (dis)?connected` | regexp `(?:\]: (?:\x1b\[[0-9;]*m)?|\[connected player\] )(?P<player>\w{1,16})(?: \([^)]*\))? (?P<event>joined|left|has connected|has disconnected)` | player != "" | label_format online=`{{ if or (eq .event "joined") (eq .event "has connected") }}1{{ else }}0{{ end }}` | unwrap online [12h]) by (container, player)) or vector(0)
signals.re: sum(last_over_time({, container!~"minecraft-java-.*proxy"} |~ `joined the game|left the game|\[connected player\] .* has (dis)?connected` | regexp `(?:\]: (?:\x1b\[[0-9;]*m)?|\[connected player\] )(?P<player>\w{1,16})(?: \([^)]*\))? (?P<event>joined|left|has connected|has disconnected)` | player != "" | label_format online=`{{ if or (eq .event "joined") (eq .event "has connected") }}1{{ else }}0{{ end }}` | unwrap online [12h]) by (container, player)) or vector(0)

alerts.rb:
### Meaning

WordPress in {{ $labels.namespace }} is down.

The WordPress container is not ready, its PHP-FPM pool is unreachable, or a WordPress scrape target is down in {{ $labels.namespace }} ({{ $labels.cluster }}) for 5 minutes.

It fires when the expression below holds for 5m.

### Impact

Something users depend on is already broken or about to be. Treat it as an incident.

### Diagnosis

Run the alert expression and look at which series cross the threshold:

```promql
(max by (cluster, namespace) (kube_pod_container_status_ready{container=~"wordpress.*", namespace=~".*wordpress.*"}) == 0) or (max by (cluster, namespace, instance) (phpfpm_up{namespace=~".*wordpress.*"}) == 0) or (max by (cluster, namespace, job) (up{job=~".*wordpress.*", namespace=~".*wordpress.*"}) == 0)
```

Then open this board with the same selectors: the tab that carries those metrics shows how long the series has been where it is, and the restart and deploy annotations show whether a release or a restart lines up with the change.

### Mitigation

- Confirm the target is the one you think it is: check the labels on the firing series.
- Compare against the same series on a healthy peer; a single instance out of line is a different problem from every instance moving together.
- If a deploy or restart lines up with the change, that is the first thing to undo.
- If the threshold no longer matches how this service behaves, change the rule rather than living with a permanent alert.
alerts.s: WordPress in {{ $labels.namespace }} is down.

signals.d: Apache workers serving a request.
Requests per second through Apache (mod_status).
Comments in the site.

signals.d: Share of the site's responses at the ingress that are server errors. 502/504 with a healthy pod usually means PHP-FPM ran out of workers or timed out.

Requests waiting for a free worker right now.

Busy workers against the pool size.
Requests that ran longer than request_slowlog_timeout.
Workers the pool currently runs.
PHP-FPM pools the exporter can reach.
Responses per second at the ingress-nginx controller, by status code.
Slowest 5 percent of requests as the ingress measured them, WordPress render time included.

Attachments in the media library.
Open client connections on NGINX.

Pages in the site.
Installed plugins.
Posts in the site.

Installed themes.

Run the alert expression and look at which series cross the threshold:

```promql
group by (cluster) (kube_node_info) unless on (cluster) group by (cluster) (up{job=~"integrations/kubernetes/kubelet|kubelet"} == 1)
```

Then open this board with the same selectors: the tab that carries those metrics shows how long the series has been where it is, and the restart and deploy annotations show whether a release or a restart lines up with the change.

- Compare against the same series on a healthy peer; a single instance out of line is a different problem from every instance moving together.
- If a deploy or restart lines up with the change, that is the first thing to undo.
- If the threshold no longer matches how this service behaves, change the rule rather than living with a permanent alert.

alerts.d: CoreDNS {{ $labels.instance }} is down.
alerts.rb:
### Meaning

CoreDNS has disappeared from Prometheus target discovery.

CoreDNS {{ $labels.instance }} is down.

It fires when the expression below holds for 15m.

### Impact

Something users depend on is already broken or about to be. Treat it as an incident.

### Diagnosis

Run the alert expression and look at which series cross the threshold:

```promql
(up == 0) and on (job, instance) (max_over_time(coredns_build_info[1d]))
```

Then open this board with the same selectors: the tab that carries those metrics shows how long the series has been where it is, and the restart and deploy annotations show whether a release or a restart lines up with the change.

### Mitigation

- Confirm the target is the one you think it is: check the labels on the firing series.
- Compare against the same series on a healthy peer; a single instance out of line is a different problem from every instance moving together.
- If a deploy or restart lines up with the change, that is the first thing to undo.
- If the threshold no longer matches how this service behaves, change the rule rather than living with a permanent alert.
alerts.s: CoreDNS has disappeared from Prometheus target discovery.

signals.d: "Failed to connect": getting a token from the Pangolin server failed (bad credentials, TLS certificate, server unreachable).
signals.e: sum by (cluster, namespace) (count_over_time({cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} |~ `Failed to connect:` [$__auto]))

signals.d: newt_connection_errors_total: connection errors per type.
"Connecting to endpoint": a tunnel connect attempt.
signals.e: sum by (cluster, namespace) (count_over_time({cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} |~ `Connecting to endpoint` [$__auto]))

signals.d: "Tunnel connection to server established": the WireGuard tunnel to the Pangolin server came up. More than one per newt start means it is reconnecting.
signals.e: sum by (cluster, namespace) (count_over_time({cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} |~ `Tunnel connection to server established` [$__auto]))
signals.re: sum by (cluster, namespace) (count_over_time( |~ `Tunnel connection to server established` [$__auto]))

signals.d: Tunnel connects over the time range, all selected newt pods. One per pod start is normal.
signals.e: sum(count_over_time({cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} |~ `Tunnel connection to server established` [$__range])) or vector(0)
signals.re: sum(count_over_time( |~ `Tunnel connection to server established` [$__range])) or vector(0)

signals.d: "Exiting...": the newt process shut down (restart, eviction, or the server replacing this client).
Target addresses newt failed to reach, by count over the range (ClusterIP:port - map it to a Service).
signals.e: topk(20, sum by (cluster, target) (count_over_time({cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} |= `Error connecting to target` | regexp `dial tcp (?P<target>[^:]+:[0-9]+)` | target != "" [$__range])))
signals.re: topk(20, sum by (cluster, target) (count_over_time( |= `Error connecting to target` | regexp `dial tcp (?P<target>[^:]+:[0-9]+)` | target != "" [$__range])))

signals.d: "Target N: health check failed": Pangolin health checks newt runs against the targets.
signals.e: sum by (cluster, namespace) (count_over_time({cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} |~ `health check failed` [$__auto]))

signals.d: Newt container logs, minus the per-resource "Started tcp proxy" lines, the update banner and the ICMP warm-up pings.
signals.e: {cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} !~ `Started tcp proxy to|[╔╚║╠]|Ping attempt [0-9]+ failed|Initial reliable ping failed|Failed to remove health file`
signals.re: !~ `Started tcp proxy to|[╔╚║╠]|Ping attempt [0-9]+ failed|Initial reliable ping failed|Failed to remove health file`

signals.d: "Connection to server lost after N failures": the tunnel went down; newt keeps retrying.
signals.e: sum by (cluster, namespace) (count_over_time({cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} |~ `Connection to server lost` [$__auto]))
signals.re: sum by (cluster, namespace) (count_over_time( |~ `Connection to server lost` [$__auto]))

signals.d: Lost tunnels and failed connects over the time range.
signals.e: sum(count_over_time({cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} |~ `Connection to server lost|Failed to connect:` [$__range])) or vector(0)
signals.re: sum(count_over_time( |~ `Connection to server lost|Failed to connect:` [$__range])) or vector(0)

signals.d: Newt containers that exist but are not ready.
ERROR / FATAL log lines.
newt_proxy_active_connections: open proxied connections per protocol.
newt_proxy_drops_total: proxied writes dropped on errors.
Ready newt containers per cluster. 0 = the cluster has no tunnel: every resource Pangolin publishes from it is down.
Ready newt containers across the selected clusters.
Container restarts over the selected time range.
"Error connecting to target": a published resource refused or timed out when newt proxied a connection to it. The tunnel is fine; the service behind it is not.
signals.e: sum by (cluster, namespace) (count_over_time({cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} |~ `Error connecting to target|Error accepting TCP connection` [$__auto]))
signals.re: sum by (cluster, namespace) (count_over_time( |~ `Error connecting to target|Error accepting TCP connection` [$__auto]))

signals.d: Proxied connections that newt could not open to the target service, over the time range.
signals.e: sum(count_over_time({cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} |~ `Error connecting to target|Error accepting TCP connection` [$__range])) or vector(0)
signals.re: sum(count_over_time( |~ `Error connecting to target|Error accepting TCP connection` [$__range])) or vector(0)

signals.d: newt_tunnel_bytes_total: bytes through the tunnels, per direction.
newt_tunnel_latency_seconds: 95th percentile tunnel latency.
The tunnel lifecycle lines only: starts, connects, losses, failures, exits.
signals.e: {cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} |~ `Tunnel connection to server established|Websocket connected|Connection to server lost|Failed to connect:|Exiting\.\.\.|Newt version`
signals.re: |~ `Tunnel connection to server established|Websocket connected|Connection to server lost|Failed to connect:|Exiting\.\.\.|Newt version`

signals.d: newt_tunnel_sessions: active tunnel sessions.
"Websocket connected": the control channel to the Pangolin server came up.
signals.e: sum by (cluster, namespace) (count_over_time({cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace", container=~"newt"} |~ `Websocket connected` [$__auto]))

signals.d: newt_websocket_connected: control channel to the Pangolin server, 1 = connected.
newt_websocket_reconnects_total + newt_tunnel_reconnects_total: reconnects per reason.

alerts.rb:
### Meaning

Alertmanager {{ $labels.instance }} is down.

It fires when the expression below holds for 5m.

### Impact

Something users depend on is already broken or about to be. Treat it as an incident.

### Diagnosis

Run the alert expression and look at which series cross the threshold:

```promql
(up == 0) and on (job, instance) (max_over_time(alertmanager_build_info[1d]))
```

Then open this board with the same selectors: the tab that carries those metrics shows how long the series has been where it is, and the restart and deploy annotations show whether a release or a restart lines up with the change.

### Mitigation

- Confirm the target is the one you think it is: check the labels on the firing series.
- Compare against the same series on a healthy peer; a single instance out of line is a different problem from every instance moving together.
- If a deploy or restart lines up with the change, that is the first thing to undo.
- If the threshold no longer matches how this service behaves, change the rule rather than living with a permanent alert.
alerts.s: Alertmanager {{ $labels.instance }} is down.

### Meaning

Argo CD application {{ $labels.name }} ({{ $labels.project }}) has been out of sync for 30 minutes.

It fires when the expression below holds for 30m.

### Impact

Informational. It is context for another alert rather than work of its own.

### Diagnosis

Run the alert expression and look at which series cross the threshold:

```promql
sum by (name, project) (argocd_app_info{sync_status="OutOfSync"}) > 0
```

Then open this board with the same selectors: the tab that carries those metrics shows how long the series has been where it is, and the restart and deploy annotations show whether a release or a restart lines up with the change.

### Mitigation

- Confirm the target is the one you think it is: check the labels on the firing series.
- Compare against the same series on a healthy peer; a single instance out of line is a different problem from every instance moving together.
- If a deploy or restart lines up with the change, that is the first thing to undo.
- If the threshold no longer matches how this service behaves, change the rule rather than living with a permanent alert.
alerts.s: Argo CD application {{ $labels.name }} ({{ $labels.project }}) has been out of sync for 30 minutes.

services.argocd.description: Argo-cd as a service, wherever it runs: its pods, their resources and logs first, then its own metrics, then only the platform tabs that have data (Kubernetes, containers, Docker, systemd, process, ingress, Windows, logs, the Backstage catalog entry), alerts and Kubernetes event annotations.

signals.d: Every application with its project, sync and health status.
signals.e: max by (name, project, sync_status, health_status) (argocd_app_info{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace|", pod=~"$pod|"})

signals.d: Applications Argo CD manages.
Applications by health status (Healthy, Progressing, Degraded, Suspended, Missing, Unknown).
Applications by sync status (Synced, OutOfSync, Unknown).
Applications whose live state differs from git.
signals.e: sum(argocd_app_info{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace|", pod=~"$pod|", sync_status="OutOfSync"}) or vector(0)

signals.d: Applications that are Degraded, Missing, Suspended or Unknown.
signals.e: sum(argocd_app_info{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace|", pod=~"$pod|", health_status!~"Healthy|Progressing"}) or vector(0)

signals.d: Watch events received per second per cluster.
Kubernetes objects the controller caches per cluster.
Clusters registered as deployment targets.
Registered clusters the controller cannot connect to.
CPU cores used per Argo CD component pod.
Slowest 1 percent of git requests by type.
signals.e: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, request_type) (rate(argocd_git_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace|", pod=~"$pod|"}[$__rate_interval])))

signals.d: Git requests per second by type (ls-remote, fetch).
CPU cores used by the process group (all its processes summed).
Voluntary and non-voluntary context switches per second. Many non-voluntary switches mean CPU contention.
Open descriptors of the worst process divided by its soft limit. Near 1 the process starts failing with too many open files.
Open file descriptors across the process group.
Bytes read from storage by the process group per second, with writes alongside.
Bytes written to storage by the process group per second.
Major page faults per second: the process is reading pages back from disk, a sign of memory pressure.
Processes in the group. More than expected usually means forks or workers piling up.
Resident memory of the process group.
Processes of the group by kernel state (Running, Sleeping, Waiting, Zombie, Other).
Threads across the process group.
Time since the oldest process of the group started.
Requests per second by Ingress host name.
Requests per second by Ingress object.
Requests per second by HTTP method.
The ten busiest host and path combinations.
Requests per second by HTTP status code returned to the client.
Request bytes received per second (in) and response bytes sent per second (out).
Response bytes sent to clients per second.
Share of requests answered with a 4xx (client errors: auth, not found, bad requests).
Share of requests answered with a 5xx as seen at the ingress (includes upstream failures and nginx 502/503/504). The second line is the 4xx share.
Distinct host names currently serving traffic.
Distinct Ingress objects currently serving traffic.
Median request duration at the ingress.
95th percentile of request duration at the ingress.
Request duration as measured by nginx from first byte in to last byte out: p99, p95 and p50.
Requests per second arriving through ingress-nginx for the selected Ingress objects.
502/503/504 answers per second: the backend refused, was unavailable or timed out.
Slowest 1 percent of upstream (backend) response times as seen by nginx. Compare with the request p99: a gap is time spent in nginx or on the client side.
Kubernetes API requests per second by verb and response code.
signals.e: sum by (verb, response_code) (rate(argocd_app_k8s_request_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace|", pod=~"$pod|"}[$__rate_interval]))

signals.d: Time since each pod started.

CPU cores used by all containers of each pod (cAdvisor). Dashed lines are the requests and limits from kube-state-metrics: usage above the request means the pod competes for CPU, usage at the limit means it is being throttled.
CPU limit of the pod containers (above it the kernel throttles).
CPU requested by the pod containers (what the scheduler reserved).
Deployment replicas that are available (ready for minReadySeconds).
Replicas the Deployment spec asks for (dashed) versus replicas actually available.
Nodes that should run the DaemonSet pod (dashed) versus nodes where it is ready.
Nodes where the DaemonSet pod is ready.
Working-set memory of each pod (what the kernel would OOM-kill on). Dashed lines are requests and limits: a working set near the limit means an OOM kill is close.
Memory limit of the pod containers (the OOM-kill threshold).
Memory requested by the pod containers.
Pods in any phase other than Running.
Number of pods in each phase (Running, Pending, Succeeded, Failed, Unknown).
Pods matching the selection.
Used share of every PersistentVolumeClaim in the namespace, from kubelet volume stats. Not tied to a pod: the whole namespace is shown.
Containers that pass their readiness probe, per pod.
Containers currently passing their readiness probe.
Cumulative container restarts per pod. A rising line is a crash loop or a failing liveness probe.
Container restarts in the last hour across the selected pods. Anything above zero deserves a look at the Waiting reasons.
Replicas the StatefulSet spec asks for (dashed) versus replicas that are ready.
StatefulSet replicas that are ready.
Containers stuck in Waiting and why (CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, ContainerCreating...).
Containers currently in the Waiting state (not running, not terminated).
Age of the most recently started pod. A young pod on a long-running service means a restart or a rollout.
kubectl invocations waiting to run (apply, auth), by command.
Journal lines of the systemd unit on the selected hosts, from Loki.
Log lines of the selected pods, from Loki.
CPU cores used by the process, from its own /metrics (process_cpu_seconds_total).
Open file descriptors divided by the process limit. Near 1 new connections and files start failing.
signals.e: process_open_fds{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace|", pod=~"$pod|"} / process_max_fds{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace|", pod=~"$pod|"}

signals.d: File descriptors the process has open.
Resident set size reported by the process itself. The dashed line is the virtual address space size.
Time since the process started (process_start_time_seconds).
Virtual memory size of the process (address space, not RAM used).
Median application reconciliation time.
signals.e: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(argocd_app_reconcile_bucket{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace|", pod=~"$pod|"}[$__rate_interval])))

signals.d: Slowest 1 percent of application reconciliations. Long reconciles mean large apps, slow repos or a slow cluster API.
signals.e: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(argocd_app_reconcile_bucket{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace|", pod=~"$pod|"}[$__rate_interval])))

signals.d: Application reconciliations per second across the controller.
Failed Redis requests per second. Redis backs the caches; failures slow every reconcile.
Requests waiting on the repo server. A growing queue means manifest generation is the bottleneck.
Resident memory per Argo CD component pod.
Sync operations that failed or errored in the last hour.
signals.e: sum(increase(argocd_app_sync_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace|", pod=~"$pod|", phase=~"Error|Failed"}[1h])) or vector(0)

signals.d: Failed sync operations by application.
Sync operations per second by outcome phase (Succeeded, Failed, Error, Running).
Units in the active state.
Units in the failed state.
Units currently failed, by host.
Hosts that have a matching unit at all.
Units that are loaded but not running.
Service restarts (needs the collector restart metrics: --collector.systemd.enable-restarts-metrics).
State of each unit on each host: active, transitioning (activating/deactivating), inactive or failed.
signals.e: max by (instance, name) ((node_systemd_unit_state{name=~"argo-cd.service", state="active", instance=~"$host"} == 1) * 1 or (node_systemd_unit_state{name=~"argo-cd.service", state=~"activating|deactivating", instance=~"$host"} == 1) * 2 or (node_systemd_unit_state{name=~"argo-cd.service", state="inactive", instance=~"$host"} == 1) * 3 or (node_systemd_unit_state{name=~"argo-cd.service", state="failed", instance=~"$host"} == 1) * 4)
signals.re: max by (instance, name) ((node_systemd_unit_state{name=~"argo-cd.service", state="active", } == 1) * 1 or (node_systemd_unit_state{name=~"argo-cd.service", state=~"activating|deactivating", } == 1) * 2 or (node_systemd_unit_state{name=~"argo-cd.service", state="inactive", } == 1) * 3 or (node_systemd_unit_state{name=~"argo-cd.service", state="failed", } == 1) * 4)

signals.d: Tasks (threads and processes) the unit runs. Needs --collector.systemd.enable-task-metrics.
TasksMax for the unit. Hitting it blocks the unit from forking.
Tasks against the unit limit.
Time since the unit last started. A drop marks a restart.
CPU cores used by the matching Windows processes on each host.
Handles held by the matching Windows processes. Steadily growing means a handle leak.
Bytes read and written by the matching Windows processes per second, by IO mode.
State of the Windows service on every host where it exists: running, starting, paused or stopping, stopped (windows_exporter service collector).
signals.e: max by (instance, name) ((windows_service_state{name=~"(?i)argo-cd", state="running", instance=~"$host"} == 1) * 1 or (windows_service_state{name=~"(?i)argo-cd", state=~"start pending|continue pending", instance=~"$host"} == 1) * 2 or (windows_service_state{name=~"(?i)argo-cd", state=~"paused|pause pending|stop pending", instance=~"$host"} == 1) * 3 or (windows_service_state{name=~"(?i)argo-cd", state="stopped", instance=~"$host"} == 1) * 4)
signals.re: max by (instance, name) ((windows_service_state{name=~"(?i)argo-cd", state="running", } == 1) * 1 or (windows_service_state{name=~"(?i)argo-cd", state=~"start pending|continue pending", } == 1) * 2 or (windows_service_state{name=~"(?i)argo-cd", state=~"paused|pause pending|stop pending", } == 1) * 3 or (windows_service_state{name=~"(?i)argo-cd", state="stopped", } == 1) * 4)

signals.d: Threads of the matching Windows processes.
Time since the oldest matching Windows process started.
Working set of the matching Windows processes (private bytes where the exporter reports them, otherwise the shared working set).
Items waiting in each controller workqueue.
Slowest 1 percent of time items spend waiting in each workqueue.
signals.e: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, name) (rate(workqueue_queue_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace|", pod=~"$pod|"}[$__rate_interval])))

alerts.rb:
### Meaning

Grafana {{ $labels.instance }} is down.

It fires when the expression below holds for 5m.

### Impact

Something users depend on is already broken or about to be. Treat it as an incident.

### Diagnosis

Run the alert expression and look at which series cross the threshold:

```promql
(up == 0) and on (job, instance) (max_over_time(grafana_build_info[1d]))
```

Then open this board with the same selectors: the tab that carries those metrics shows how long the series has been where it is, and the restart and deploy annotations show whether a release or a restart lines up with the change.

### Mitigation

- Confirm the target is the one you think it is: check the labels on the firing series.
- Compare against the same series on a healthy peer; a single instance out of line is a different problem from every instance moving together.
- If a deploy or restart lines up with the change, that is the first thing to undo.
- If the threshold no longer matches how this service behaves, change the rule rather than living with a permanent alert.
alerts.s: Grafana {{ $labels.instance }} is down.

### Meaning

Request p99 latency on {{ $labels.instance }} is above 1s.

It fires when the expression below holds for 15m.

### Impact

Nothing is broken yet, and it will be if the trend holds. Look at it this working day.

### Diagnosis

Run the alert expression and look at which series cross the threshold:

```promql
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le)(rate(pyroscope_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) > 1
```

Then open this board with the same selectors: the tab that carries those metrics shows how long the series has been where it is, and the restart and deploy annotations show whether a release or a restart lines up with the change.

### Mitigation

- Confirm the target is the one you think it is: check the labels on the firing series.
- Compare against the same series on a healthy peer; a single instance out of line is a different problem from every instance moving together.
- If a deploy or restart lines up with the change, that is the first thing to undo.
- If the threshold no longer matches how this service behaves, change the rule rather than living with a permanent alert.

services.pyroscope.description: Pyroscope as a service, wherever it runs: its pods, their resources and logs first, then its own metrics, then only the platform tabs that have data (Kubernetes, containers, Docker, systemd, process, ingress, Windows, logs, the Backstage catalog entry), alerts and Kubernetes event annotations.

signals.d: CPU cores used by the process group (all its processes summed).
Voluntary and non-voluntary context switches per second. Many non-voluntary switches mean CPU contention.
Open descriptors of the worst process divided by its soft limit. Near 1 the process starts failing with too many open files.
Open file descriptors across the process group.
Bytes read from storage by the process group per second, with writes alongside.
Bytes written to storage by the process group per second.
Major page faults per second: the process is reading pages back from disk, a sign of memory pressure.
Processes in the group. More than expected usually means forks or workers piling up.
Resident memory of the process group.
Processes of the group by kernel state (Running, Sleeping, Waiting, Zombie, Other).
Threads across the process group.
Time since the oldest process of the group started.
Requests per second by Ingress host name.
Requests per second by Ingress object.
Requests per second by HTTP method.
The ten busiest host and path combinations.
Requests per second by HTTP status code returned to the client.
Request bytes received per second (in) and response bytes sent per second (out).
Response bytes sent to clients per second.
Share of requests answered with a 4xx (client errors: auth, not found, bad requests).
Share of requests answered with a 5xx as seen at the ingress (includes upstream failures and nginx 502/503/504). The second line is the 4xx share.
Distinct host names currently serving traffic.
Distinct Ingress objects currently serving traffic.
Median request duration at the ingress.
95th percentile of request duration at the ingress.
Request duration as measured by nginx from first byte in to last byte out: p99, p95 and p50.
Requests per second arriving through ingress-nginx for the selected Ingress objects.
502/503/504 answers per second: the backend refused, was unavailable or timed out.
Slowest 1 percent of upstream (backend) response times as seen by nginx. Compare with the request p99: a gap is time spent in nginx or on the client side.
Time since each pod started.

CPU cores used by all containers of each pod (cAdvisor). Dashed lines are the requests and limits from kube-state-metrics: usage above the request means the pod competes for CPU, usage at the limit means it is being throttled.
CPU limit of the pod containers (above it the kernel throttles).
CPU requested by the pod containers (what the scheduler reserved).
Deployment replicas that are available (ready for minReadySeconds).
Replicas the Deployment spec asks for (dashed) versus replicas actually available.
Nodes that should run the DaemonSet pod (dashed) versus nodes where it is ready.
Nodes where the DaemonSet pod is ready.
Working-set memory of each pod (what the kernel would OOM-kill on). Dashed lines are requests and limits: a working set near the limit means an OOM kill is close.
Memory limit of the pod containers (the OOM-kill threshold).
Memory requested by the pod containers.
Pods in any phase other than Running.
Number of pods in each phase (Running, Pending, Succeeded, Failed, Unknown).
Pods matching the selection.
Used share of every PersistentVolumeClaim in the namespace, from kubelet volume stats. Not tied to a pod: the whole namespace is shown.
Containers that pass their readiness probe, per pod.
Containers currently passing their readiness probe.
Cumulative container restarts per pod. A rising line is a crash loop or a failing liveness probe.
Container restarts in the last hour across the selected pods. Anything above zero deserves a look at the Waiting reasons.
Replicas the StatefulSet spec asks for (dashed) versus replicas that are ready.
StatefulSet replicas that are ready.
Containers stuck in Waiting and why (CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, ContainerCreating...).
Containers currently in the Waiting state (not running, not terminated).
Age of the most recently started pod. A young pod on a long-running service means a restart or a rollout.

histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le)(rate(pyroscope_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespace|", pod=~"$pod|"}[$__rate_interval])))

Resident set size reported by the process itself. The dashed line is the virtual address space size.
Time since the process started (process_start_time_seconds).
Virtual memory size of the process (address space, not RAM used).
Units in the active state.
Units in the failed state.
Units currently failed, by host.
Hosts that have a matching unit at all.
Units that are loaded but not running.

State of each unit on each host: active, transitioning (activating/deactivating), inactive or failed.

alerts.rb:
### Meaning

cAdvisor on {{ $labels.instance }} is down.

It fires when the expression below holds for 5m.

### Impact

Something users depend on is already broken or about to be. Treat it as an incident.

### Diagnosis

Run the alert expression and look at which series cross the threshold:

```promql
(up == 0) and on (job, instance) (max_over_time(cadvisor_version_info[1d]))
```

Then open this board with the same selectors: the tab that carries those metrics shows how long the series has been where it is, and the restart and deploy annotations show whether a release or a restart lines up with the change.

### Mitigation

- Confirm the target is the one you think it is: check the labels on the firing series.
- Compare against the same series on a healthy peer; a single instance out of line is a different problem from every instance moving together.
- If a deploy or restart lines up with the change, that is the first thing to undo.
- If the threshold no longer matches how this service behaves, change the rule rather than living with a permanent alert.
alerts.s: cAdvisor on {{ $labels.instance }} is down.

system.linux.description: One Linux host from node_exporter: facts and health tiles, then CPU, memory, disk, network, temperature and pressure rows, plus exporter tabs that appear only where their metrics exist (Proxmox, Docker, kubelet, Batocera, ZFS, NFS, battery, services, updates, logs).

signals.d: Batocera release running on this host.
Hardware temperatures on Batocera hosts.
Battery charge in percent.
AC adapter connected (1) or on battery (0).
Power drawn from or delivered to the battery.
Battery voltage.
Time until each monitored certificate expires.
Connection-tracking table size.
Connection-tracking entries in use against the table limit (dashed). At the limit new connections are dropped.
Context switches per second. A jump with flat load means threads fighting over locks or IO.
Share of CPU time not idle, averaged over all cores.
Average current CPU frequency across cores. Pinned low under load means power capping or thermal throttling.
CPU time by mode (user, system, iowait, steal, irq...), stacked. Growing iowait means the disks are the bottleneck, steal means the hypervisor is.
Share of time each device was busy with IO. Near 1 the device is saturated.
Weighted time spent doing IO per second: queue depth times service time. Rises before throughput drops.
Bytes read and written per second per block device.
Read and write operations completed per second per block device.
Bytes written per second per block device.
Write operations completed per second per block device.
Containers cAdvisor sees on this host.
CPU cores used per container on this host.
Memory used per container on this host.
Entropy available to the kernel random pool.
Kernel-wide file descriptor limit.
File descriptors allocated system-wide against the kernel maximum (dashed).
Free bytes on each filesystem, as available to non-root users.
Size of each filesystem.
Used share of each mounted filesystem.
Batocera game packages installed.
Batocera game packages with pending updates.
signals.e: batocerapkg_updates_pending{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"} or pacman_updates_pending{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}

signals.d: Used share of inodes per filesystem. A full inode table stops file creation with space still free.
Time until each apt repository signing key expires. Expired keys silently break updates.
Run-queue length averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare with the core count: above it, processes wait for CPU.
Load average over 15 minutes.
Load average over 5 minutes.
1-minute load divided by the number of cores. Above 1 the host is saturated.
signals.e: node_load1{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"} / count without (cpu, mode) (node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle",job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"})

signals.d: Memory the kernel estimates it can give to new work without swapping, including reclaimable cache.
Kernel buffers for block devices.
Page cache. Reclaimable, so not a leak.
Completely unused memory. Low is normal on Linux: the kernel uses it for cache.
Memory in use (total minus available), with page cache, buffers and free memory alongside. Cache and buffers are reclaimable.
Memory in use as a share of total, counting reclaimable cache as available.
Bytes received and transmitted per second per interface.
Packets dropped per second on receive and transmit. Receive drops usually mean the host cannot keep up with the NIC.
Receive and transmit errors per second per interface. Any sustained value points at a cable, driver or duplex problem.
Total bytes received and transmitted per second, loopback excluded.
Bytes transmitted per second per interface.
Packets dropped per second on transmit.
Transmit errors per second per interface.
Total bytes transmitted per second, loopback excluded.
NFS RPC retransmissions per second. Above zero the NFS server or the network is lagging.
NFS client RPC calls per second.
systemd journal of this host, from Loki.
Time since the package lists were last refreshed.
Minor and major page faults per second. Major faults read from disk and hurt.
Major page faults per second.
Processes in uninterruptible sleep, almost always waiting for disk IO.
Processes currently runnable.
Share of time some tasks waited for a CPU (pressure stall information).
Share of time some tasks (some) and all tasks (full) stalled on IO.
Share of time every task was stalled on IO.
Share of time some tasks (some) and all tasks (full) stalled on memory.
Share of time every task was stalled on memory.
vCPUs allocated to guests on this Proxmox node.
Memory allocated to guests on this Proxmox node.
Proxmox VE reports the node online.
CPU package power draw from RAPL counters.
The package manager flagged that a reboot is needed (new kernel or libc).
Time runnable tasks spent waiting for a CPU per second, summed over cores.
systemd units in the active state.
systemd units in the failed state.
Memory used by TCP socket buffers.
TCP sockets in use.
Packets dropped and softirq budget exhaustions (squeezed) per second in the network receive path.
Times the softirq receive budget ran out per second.
Pages swapped in and out per second. Any sustained swapping means memory pressure.
Pages paged in and out from block devices per second (all IO through the page cache, not just swap).

signals.d: Outgoing TCP connections opened per second.

alerts.rb:
### Meaning

Process group {{ $labels.groupname }} on {{ $labels.instance }} has a process at more than 80% of its file descriptor limit.

It fires when the expression below holds for 15m.

### Impact

Nothing is broken yet, and it will be if the trend holds. Look at it this working day.

### Diagnosis

Run the alert expression and look at which series cross the threshold:

```promql
namedprocess_namegroup_worst_fd_ratio > 0.8
```

Then open this board with the same selectors: the tab that carries those metrics shows how long the series has been where it is, and the restart and deploy annotations show whether a release or a restart lines up with the change.

### Mitigation

- Confirm the target is the one you think it is: check the labels on the firing series.
- Compare against the same series on a healthy peer; a single instance out of line is a different problem from every instance moving together.
- If a deploy or restart lines up with the change, that is the first thing to undo.
- If the threshold no longer matches how this service behaves, change the rule rather than living with a permanent alert.

system.processExporter.description: Process groups from process-exporter: CPU, memory, processes and threads, file descriptors, IO and page faults per group and host, top-N tables and scrape health.

signals.d: CPU cores used by the process group (all its processes summed).
Voluntary and non-voluntary context switches per second. Many non-voluntary switches mean CPU contention.
signals.e: sum by (instance, groupname, ctxswitchtype) (rate(namedprocess_namegroup_context_switches_total{groupname=~".*", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", groupname=~"$groupname"}[$__rate_interval]))

signals.d: Open descriptors of the worst process divided by its soft limit. Near 1 the process starts failing with too many open files.
signals.e: max by (instance, groupname) (namedprocess_namegroup_worst_fd_ratio{groupname=~".*", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", groupname=~"$groupname"})

signals.d: Open file descriptors across the process group.
signals.e: sum by (instance, groupname) (namedprocess_namegroup_open_filedesc{groupname=~".*", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", groupname=~"$groupname"})

signals.d: Bytes read from storage by the process group per second, with writes alongside.
Bytes written to storage by the process group per second.
Major page faults per second: the process is reading pages back from disk, a sign of memory pressure.
Processes in the group. More than expected usually means forks or workers piling up.
signals.e: sum by (instance, groupname) (namedprocess_namegroup_num_procs{groupname=~".*", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", groupname=~"$groupname"})

signals.d: Resident memory of the process group.
signals.e: sum by (instance, groupname) (namedprocess_namegroup_memory_bytes{groupname=~".*", memtype="resident", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", groupname=~"$groupname"})

signals.d: process-exporter scrape errors per second (full, partial and /proc read errors). Usually permissions on /proc.
Processes of the group by kernel state (Running, Sleeping, Waiting, Zombie, Other).
signals.e: sum by (instance, groupname, state) (namedprocess_namegroup_states{groupname=~".*", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", groupname=~"$groupname"})

signals.d: Threads across the process group.
signals.e: sum by (instance, groupname) (namedprocess_namegroup_num_threads{groupname=~".*", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", groupname=~"$groupname"})

signals.d: The ten process groups using the most CPU on the selected hosts.
The ten process groups using the most resident memory on the selected hosts.
signals.e: topk(10, sum by (instance, groupname) (namedprocess_namegroup_memory_bytes{memtype="resident", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}))

signals.d: Time since the oldest process of the group started.
signals.e: time() - min by (instance, groupname) (namedprocess_namegroup_oldest_start_time_seconds{groupname=~".*", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", groupname=~"$groupname"})

system.systemd.description: systemd units from node_exporter: unit state over time, active and failed counts, failed units, restarts and the overall system state.

signals.d: Units in the active state.
signals.e: count(node_systemd_unit_state{name=~".*", state="active", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"} == 1) or vector(0)

signals.d: Units in the failed state.
signals.e: count(node_systemd_unit_state{name=~".*", state="failed", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"} == 1) or vector(0)

signals.d: Units currently failed, by host.

Units that are loaded but not running.

signals.d: Service restarts (needs the collector restart metrics: --collector.systemd.enable-restarts-metrics).
1 when systemd reports the system as running, 0 when degraded (a unit failed at boot or since).

signals.d: Tasks (threads and processes) the unit runs. Needs --collector.systemd.enable-task-metrics.
TasksMax for the unit. Hitting it blocks the unit from forking.
Tasks against the unit limit.
Loaded units by state, all units on the host (not just the selected regex).
Time since the unit last started. A drop marks a restart.

signals.d: Share of requests answered with a 5xx as seen at the ingress (includes upstream failures and nginx 502/503/504). The second line is the 4xx share.
signals.e: sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", namespace=~"$ingress_namespace", ingress=~"$ingress", status=~"5.."}[$__rate_interval])) / sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", namespace=~"$ingress_namespace", ingress=~"$ingress"}[$__rate_interval]))

signals.d: Distinct host names currently serving traffic.
signals.e: count(count by (host) (nginx_ingress_controller_requests{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", namespace=~"$ingress_namespace", ingress=~"$ingress"}))

signals.d: Distinct Ingress objects currently serving traffic.
signals.e: count(count by (namespace, ingress) (nginx_ingress_controller_requests{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", namespace=~"$ingress_namespace", ingress=~"$ingress"}))

signals.d: Median request duration at the ingress.
signals.e: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", namespace=~"$ingress_namespace", ingress=~"$ingress"}[$__rate_interval])))

signals.d: 95th percentile of request duration at the ingress.
signals.e: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", namespace=~"$ingress_namespace", ingress=~"$ingress"}[$__rate_interval])))

signals.d: Request duration as measured by nginx from first byte in to last byte out: p99, p95 and p50.
signals.e: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", namespace=~"$ingress_namespace", ingress=~"$ingress"}[$__rate_interval])))

signals.d: Requests per second arriving through ingress-nginx for the selected Ingress objects.
502/503/504 answers per second: the backend refused, was unavailable or timed out.
signals.e: sum by (status) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", namespace=~"$ingress_namespace", ingress=~"$ingress", status=~"502|503|504"}[$__rate_interval]))

signals.d: Slowest 1 percent of upstream (backend) response times as seen by nginx. Compare with the request p99: a gap is time spent in nginx or on the client side.
signals.e: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_response_duration_seconds_bucket{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", namespace=~"$ingress_namespace", ingress=~"$ingress"}[$__rate_interval])))

signals.d: Connections currently open.
signals.e: label_replace(label_replace(sum by (instance) (nginx_connections_active{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}), "target", "$1", "instance", "(.*)"), "kind", "server", "", "") or label_replace(label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="active"}), "target", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"), "kind", "ingress controller", "", "")
signals.re: label_replace(label_replace(sum by (instance) (nginx_connections_active), "target", "$1", "instance", "(.*)"), "kind", "server", "", "") or label_replace(label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections{, state="active"}), "target", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"), "kind", "ingress controller", "", "")

signals.d: Share of requests answered with a 5xx (ingress controllers only: stub status has no status codes).
signals.e: label_replace(label_replace((sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", status=~"5.."}[$__rate_interval])) or 0 * sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval]))) / clamp_min(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])), 1e-9), "target", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"), "kind", "ingress controller", "", "")
signals.re: label_replace(label_replace((sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{, status=~"5.."}[5m])) or 0 * sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests[5m]))) / clamp_min(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests[5m])), 1e-9), "target", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"), "kind", "ingress controller", "", "")

signals.d: 95th percentile request duration (ingress controllers only).
Requests per second handled by the NGINX.
signals.e: label_replace(label_replace(sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_http_requests_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])), "target", "$1", "instance", "(.*)"), "kind", "server", "", "") or label_replace(label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_requests_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])), "target", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"), "kind", "ingress controller", "", "")
signals.re: label_replace(label_replace(sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_http_requests_total[5m])), "target", "$1", "instance", "(.*)"), "kind", "server", "", "") or label_replace(label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_requests_total[5m])), "target", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"), "kind", "ingress controller", "", "")

signals.d: 1 while the stub status answers (server) or the controller reports its build info (ingress controller).
signals.e: label_replace(label_replace(max by (instance) (nginx_up{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}), "target", "$1", "instance", "(.*)"), "kind", "server", "", "") or label_replace(label_replace(max by (controller_pod) (nginx_ingress_controller_build_info{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}), "target", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"), "kind", "ingress controller", "", "")
signals.re: label_replace(label_replace(max by (instance) (nginx_up), "target", "$1", "instance", "(.*)"), "kind", "server", "", "") or label_replace(label_replace(max by (controller_pod) (nginx_ingress_controller_build_info), "target", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"), "kind", "ingress controller", "", "")

signals.d: Connections accepted per second.
signals.e: (sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_connections_accepted{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval]))) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="accepted"}[$__rate_interval])), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)")

signals.d: Connections currently open, including idle keep-alive ones.
signals.e: (sum by (instance) (nginx_connections_active{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"})) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="active"}), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)")

signals.d: Connections open over every NGINX shown.
signals.e: sum((sum by (instance) (nginx_connections_active{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"})) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="active"}), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"))
signals.re: sum((sum by (instance) (nginx_connections_active)) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections{, state="active"}), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"))

signals.d: Accepted minus handled: connections NGINX let go.
signals.e: (sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_connections_accepted{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])) - sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_connections_handled{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval]))) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="accepted"}[$__rate_interval])) - sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="handled"}[$__rate_interval])), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)")
signals.re: (sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_connections_accepted[5m])) - sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_connections_handled[5m]))) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections_total{, state="accepted"}[5m])) - sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections_total{, state="handled"}[5m])), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)")

signals.d: Connections accepted but not handled, per second, over every NGINX shown.
signals.e: sum((sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_connections_accepted{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])) - sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_connections_handled{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval]))) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="accepted"}[$__rate_interval])) - sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="handled"}[$__rate_interval])), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"))
signals.re: sum((sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_connections_accepted[5m])) - sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_connections_handled[5m]))) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections_total{, state="accepted"}[5m])) - sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections_total{, state="handled"}[5m])), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"))

signals.d: Connections handled per second. Lower than accepted means connections were dropped, usually at a resource limit.
signals.e: (sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_connections_handled{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval]))) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="handled"}[$__rate_interval])), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)")

signals.d: Connections where NGINX is reading the request.
signals.e: (sum by (instance) (nginx_connections_reading{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"})) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="reading"}), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)")

signals.d: Requests per second per NGINX: nginx_http_requests_total from the stub status, or the controller's own nginx process counter.
signals.e: (sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_http_requests_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval]))) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_requests_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)")

signals.d: Requests served per connection: how well keep-alive is working.
signals.e: (sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_http_requests_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_connections_handled{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.001)) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_requests_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="handled"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.001), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)")
signals.re: (sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_http_requests_total[5m])) / clamp_min(sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_connections_handled[5m])), 0.001)) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_requests_total[5m])) / clamp_min(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections_total{, state="handled"}[5m])), 0.001), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)")

signals.d: Requests per second over every NGINX shown.
signals.e: sum((sum by (instance) (rate(nginx_http_requests_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval]))) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (rate(nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_requests_total{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)"))

signals.d: NGINX servers whose stub status the exporter can read, plus running ingress-nginx controllers.
signals.e: (sum(nginx_up{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}) or vector(0)) + (count(nginx_ingress_controller_build_info{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"}) or vector(0))

signals.d: Idle keep-alive connections.
signals.e: (sum by (instance) (nginx_connections_waiting{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"})) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="waiting"}), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)")

signals.d: Connections where NGINX is writing a response.
signals.e: (sum by (instance) (nginx_connections_writing{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance"})) or label_replace(sum by (controller_pod) (nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections{job=~"$job", cluster=~"$cluster", instance=~"$instance", state="writing"}), "instance", "$1", "controller_pod", "(.*)")

webservers.nginx.title: NGINX
